My erstwhile neighbors, lovely folks—an Omaha beach sailor and his wartime Angel of Mercy bride—got themselves a Basenji in their sunset years, a pretty girl they named Tulip. “She’s a descendant of the dogs Egyptian pharaohs kept,” Dick used to tell me. “Basenjis were bred not to bark in keeping with the dignity of the royal palace.” Upon which Tulip would let loose at a random jack rabbit, bird, moth, or nothing at all. “Tulip didn’t get the memo,” Dick would add ruefully. 

Their property abutted ours. One day, we came home to find that Dick had fenced in a portion of his, right up to our property line. Suddenly there was a chain link fence running through the junipers. “Surprisingly… unneighborly,” my husband said, what with there being no chain link fences anywhere in our little town. Our houses bordered the National Forest line, and neither mountain lions nor bears appreciated metal obstacles. Then we saw the gate built into the fence, opening up onto a straight shot to our rear deck. Sure enough, Dick and Tulip came through that gate not an hour later, bearing a good bottle of NM Riesling and the good news:

“Did you see the enclosure I had built so our dogs could play without bothering the bears?”

And play they did. We let them out through their respective gates on the side of each properties and let the Basenji/Australian Cattle Dog Games begin. 

The representatives of both breeds could outyap a nervous Pomeranian. Tulip didn’t give a fig about courtly manners.
